title: A Farewell to Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) as the Most Profitable Part of American Healthcare
subtitle: Oh my God, the Consolidated Appropriations act of 2026 is unbelievable.
body_html:
Readers of this newsletter will be aware that pharmacy benefit managers exist. If you're an OG reader, you're gonna remember my classic columns like SopranoRx, where I compare pharmacy benefit managers unfavorably to the Mafia:

“PBMs are modern gangsters”

This story’s racketeers? They’ve gotten smarter, more adept, more difficult to crack—and vastly more profitable. Transparency is the enemy of good scams. With Transparency, one can tell. So there is a code, culture, and penalties for speaking out against organizations making all the money. Some people have much to lose. And this time, It’s all legal!

Well, with the passage of this year's consolidated appropriations act, hereafter CA 2026, that transparency is here, written into law, and signed by the president last night.

I'll do a quick summary to catch everybody up.

Drugs are made by pharmaceutical companies. Drugs are dispensed by pharmacies. Drugs are covered by health insurance plans. Pharmacy benefit managers don't dispense drugs, they don't make drugs, they don't sell drugs. They position drugs into different “tiers” on your formulary. This determines what co-pay you're gonna get hit with if you're a customer at a pharmacy. For this service, historically, PBMs somehow became legally able to provide rebates, which is the same thing as a kickback, but it's not criminal. PBMs ran a legal protection racket for Pharma and insurance companies at the same time: if you want your drug to sell,

“it's gotta be in a preferred tier.”

If you prescribe the generic, maybe that's not a preferred tier, and the patient would have to pay more. If you want your drug to sell—yeah, you, pharma company— the PBM can put it in a preferred tier. Therefore, it is less expensive to the end customer, and so the health plan may pay hundreds or thousands of dollars for the drug, but the patient, at the point-of-sale, and the physician at the point of prescribing, are either going to have a huge hassle and expense to chose the less preferred drug. It may be be vastly less expensive, or they can just relent, and accept that healthcare is expensive, and there's nothing they can do to change it.

Or at least, that was the status quo. And, as soon as this law kicks into force in 2028, it will no longer be the status quo.

In fact, rebates, which used to line the pockets of insurance executives—keep in mind the three largest pharmacy benefit managers in the country are express scripts, owned by CIGNA, OptumRx, owned by UnitedHealth Group, and CVS Caremark, owned by CVS Health, which also owns Aetna.

80% of the PBM market was controlled by a subsidiary of the largest healthcare companies on earth, who also owned many of the pharmacies, and who also owned the health insurance plans, and in many cases, who also owned the physician groups.

What does this new law say now?


               TITLE VII--LOWERING PRESCRIPTION DRUG COSTS

Sec. 6701. Oversight of pharmacy benefit management services.
Sec. 6702. Full rebate pass through to plan; exception for innocent plan 
          fiduciaries.
Sec. 6703. Increasing transparency in generic drug applications.

Let’s look…oh…my….they have to exhaustively list the price of every drug. the wholesale cost. The rebate. The “full price:”

 with respect to each drug dispensed, for 
                each type of dispensing channel (including retail, mail 
                order, or specialty pharmacy)--

                        ``(aa) whether such drug is a brand name drug 
                    or a generic drug, and--
                            ``(AA) in the case of a brand name drug, 
                        the wholesale acquisition cost, listed as cost 
                        per days supply and cost per dosage unit, on 
                        the date such drug was dispensed...

The actual names of the drug:

(IV) the proprietary name, established name or 
                proper name, and the National Drug Code;

The spread price—or, in legalease: 

``(III) for each such claim, the difference between 
                the amount paid under subclause (I) and the amount paid 
                under subclause (II);

Oh my Gawd— they specify everything in this law. There's no place for the PBM to hide. This law was written by someone who knew exactly what a PBM was. Who actually understand what they did. Somebody with some actual expertise wrote this law. And, it demands every dollar of a rebate, get past back to the health plan, and the beneficiaries of that health plan, and can't be stuck into the pockets of anybody along the way if the actual service they are providing is not enumerated, and in the fiduciary interest of the plan member.

That word— fiduciary—is really important. It means you have to act in the best interest of the person who is covered by the health plan. This is the point of ERISA, it's a law that provides for the tax exempt status of health benefits. But that tax exempt status comes with the full weight of the Department of Labor behind it. And whoever wrote this law—and by the way, if you're that person, feel free to reach out to me, I'd love to talk to you!—really understood what they were trying to tackle here, and in my opinion, completely destroyed the financial rationale for PBMs as a profit center for giant healthcare conglomerates.

I've never read the word “sub-clause” with more excitement in my entire life.

For years, pharmacy benefit managers have been hiding fees from both the companies buying them, and the people getting the drugs, that that's you and me, using obscure pricing schemes. Now one of those obscure pricing schemes is enumerated under the law, and it is the duty of employers to not do that, if it's not in the interest of the person who's getting the prescription at the end of the day.

(XI) the total amount received, or expected to be 
                received, by the entity providing pharmacy benefit 
                management services, from applicable entities, in 
                rebates, fees, alternative discounts, or other 
                remuneration from such entities--

Either I'm missing something, or everybody else is missing something because this is complicated, but I'm a little surprised the share price of major insurance companies like UnitedHealth Group did not drop a stone today. Granted, this is a dense law, and most people are not gonna be on top of it.

There are also some gems in this law, like the fact that you can't even renew an old contract after the 30 months is up from the passage of the law. It doesn't matter what you signed before. You have to sign a new thing that complies with this law.

The PBM game is up.

CA2026 is to PBM scams, sorry, business models, what RICO was to the Italian American Mafia. The mafia worked because of a code of silence, Omerta, that the RICO statutes helped erode. CA2026 provide provides the kind of transparency that no racket can withstand.

The penalties are steep—$10,000 a day for non-adherence per plan, and $100,000 per knowingly false item. They're not catastrophically steep. But is catastrophic is the requirement for 100% of rebates to be passed on to the health plan. If health insurance companies want to keep PBM dollars, they have to justify them, and those justifications need to be presented in plain language to both the plan sponsor and the plan member—that's a patient—like you and me! Everyone needs to be able to read those disclosures, in both plain language and machine readable formats, and they need to be provided up to four times a year.

Historically, drugs were bundled into categories, and you couldn't figure out which was which, and they didn't necessarily tell you, which was generic, which was on label, and the report would just say something like “antipsychotics”—never mind that some are $2000 a month, and some are $2 a month.

And that's…all over with.

I don't know if this is gonna actually change things, I've lived in this country and dealt with American healthcare long enough to know that the status quote is gonna fight to preserve itself. I just don't know if they have the juice anymore.

PBMs have become radioactive politically, and have become extremely popular for politicians to hate. The worm has turned…maybe.

There's a lot more in this law, and I am not gonna get into it and it's entirety right now, because it just came out and I have to read it more thoroughly. There are exciting updates about mental health parity and other items as well.

They jammed a lot in an Appropriations Act, again.

Oh, it applies to Medicare, too:

Under the amendment, PBMs would be required to pass through 100% of rebates, fees, and other remuneration to the payer. Failure to comply would allow CMS to impose monetary penalties. CMS will also have to define and enforce “reasonable and relevant” Medicare Part D contract terms related to PBM transparency around reimbursement and dispensing fees, as well as establish an appeals process for pharmacies to dispute contract terms deemed unreasonable or irrelevant.

Gulp.

Thanks for reading.

As an aside, dear readers, it is my privilege to inform you of things both boring and important. I appreciate the time you've been reading any of this, and I have over 8000 subscribers, and 3 million reads of this newsletter that tell me I'm on the right track. Thank you for reading, thank you for sharing, and encourage you to tell your world that there is something useful on these Internet pages. The Frontier Psychiatrists…out!
